# Codex book and finding aids (`codex_book`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/communication.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Communication & information (`communication`)
- Deps: helped by paper, alphabet_writing
- Core idea: Fold sheets into gatherings, sew them together along the fold and bind them between boards: the book can be written on both sides, opened at any place, carried and stacked, and lasts. Then add tools for finding: numbered pages or leaves, chapter headings, running heads, a table of contents, spaces between words, punctuation and an alphabetical index giving page numbers. With these a reader can look something up in a minute instead of unrolling a scroll from the start, and read silently and fast.
- Pitfalls:
  - Making an index without fixed page numbers: in hand-copied books pages differ from copy to copy, so indexes refer to chapters; printing made page indexes useful
  - Assuming the ancients could only read aloud: silent reading is attested in antiquity, the Augustine-and-Ambrose story is over-read
  - Thinking the codex replaced the scroll because of paper: Roman codices were parchment or papyrus; the change came first among Christians
  - Forgetting that alphabetical order itself must be taught and agreed before an index works
- History: rome: late 1st c. AD – Martial advertises his poems in pocket parchment codices; 2nd–4th c. Christians prefer the codex; by c. AD 400 codices outnumber rolls; china: bamboo-slip and silk scrolls; 10th–14th c. butterfly and wrapped-back bindings of printed sheets; Ming thread-stitched binding; india: palm-leaf books (pothi) strung on cords through holes, used for two millennia; islamic: 7th–8th c. – parchment codex Qurans; from the 9th c. paper books in Baghdad, with tables of contents and catchwords; americas: Maya and Mexica screenfold books of bark paper coated with lime; the Dresden Codex probably dates from the 11th–13th c.; europe: 7th–8th c. – Irish and Anglo-Saxon scribes separate words; 13th c. alphabetical subject indexes and the Dominican Bible concordance (c. 1230s); 1470 first printed leaf numbers (Cologne)
- Read:
  - Colin H. Roberts & T. C. Skeat, The Birth of the Codex (1983)
  - Paul Saenger, Space Between Words: The Origins of Silent Reading (1997)
  - Dennis Duncan, Index, A History of the (2021)
